addressed_problems.content: The paper evaluates ownership verification schemes on ResNet-20, ResNet-18, and ResNet-50 using CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, but all experiments were conducted as single trials due to resource constraints. As acknowledged by the authors, this leaves the statistical reproducibility and uncertainty of the results uncharacterized. An open question is how the performance of the proposed verification methods (e.g., test accuracy after embedding, robustness to pruning and fine-tuning) varies across different random seeds, initializations, and data splits. Future work should systematically repeat experiments multiple times to provide confidence intervals and quantify the variance, thereby establishing the reliability and generalizability of the lottery verification framework.

Scheme V₁ protects the sparse mask by splitting it into key masks and locked masks, which must be stored, distributed, and merged by legitimate users to recover the full winning ticket. This imposes additional storage and handling responsibilities, and the security of the scheme depends on the key masks being small yet causing a significant performance gap when missing. The paper explores various scoring functions and relative sparsity levels, but the exact optimal trade-off between key size (which affects storage cost and security) and the performance degradation (the fidelity gap) remains to be determined. An open practical question is how to minimize key size while ensuring that the performance of the model without the key mask is degraded below a pre-defined threshold (e.g., 1% accuracy drop) and that the key masks are robust to ambiguity attacks such as random key forging.

Scheme V₂ embeds a QR-code signature into the sparse mask of the winning ticket, enabling ownership verification by extracting the signature from the mask. However, this verification requires white-box access to the model's weights, which is not always available in deployment scenarios where only a black-box API is provided. This white-box limitation is a significant constraint on the applicability of Scheme V₂. An unresolved issue is how to extend mask-based verification to black-box settings without relying on additional trigger sets, or how to design methods that can verify ownership with limited or only partial access to the model weights, while retaining the robustness properties of the mask embedding.

Scheme V₃ combines mask embedding with a trigger set to enable black-box verification, allowing ownership to be claimed by querying the model on trigger images and checking predictions. The paper uses a specific trigger set from prior work and demonstrates high detection rates with minimal impact on main-task accuracy. However, the design of trigger sets that maximize detection power while minimizing performance degradation on the original task and resisting ambiguity attacks (e.g., forging fake trigger sets) requires further systematic study. Open questions include how trigger set size, image composition, label assignment, and training schedule affect the trade-off between verification accuracy and model utility, and how to make the trigger set robust against adaptive adversaries who might attempt to remove or spoof the backdoor.

The paper embeds the QR-code signature into low-level convolutional layers of the winning ticket because these layers are empirically less sparse and thus more robust to pruning attacks that could distort the signature. However, this choice is heuristic and the optimal selection of layers, signature sizes (e.g., QR-code version), and error-correction parameters (e.g., correction level) to maximize robustness against adaptive removal attacks (fine-tuning, pruning, add-on attacks) remains an open practical question. Future work should systematically investigate how the location and properties of the embedded signature interact with the sparsity structure of the winning ticket and the attack strategies, in order to develop guidelines for robust mask embedding that can withstand a wide range of adversarial manipulations.

Deep neural networks contain highly over-parameterized models whose practical use motivates identifying much smaller sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) that can be trained to match dense-model performance. State-of-the-art methods for finding such winning tickets (notably iterative magnitude pruning, IMP) require repeated train–prune–retrain cycles and therefore incur very large computational cost, so a discovered winning ticket is a costly, scarce asset. At the same time, prior ownership-verification and watermarking techniques for neural networks have focused on embedding signatures in dense model weights (via regularizers or passports) or in model predictions (trigger sets/backdoors). These existing techniques do not exploit the sparse topological information that is the essential, value-bearing object for winning tickets. Consequently, there is no established, systematic framework for (a) formally defining ownership verification specifically for extremely sparse winning tickets, (b) embedding owner-specific credentials into sparse masks so the credential survives common model manipulations, and (c) performing verification in both white-box and black-box settings while resisting removal (pruning, fine-tuning) and ambiguity (reverse-engineering, forged-signature) attacks. This gap prevents certificate-like protection of winning tickets and leaves owners unable to reliably claim or detect unauthorized re-use of their computationally expensive sparse models.

nodes.content: The ownership-protection literature lacked a tailored, formal specification for the problem of verifying ownership of extremely sparse winning tickets. Prior verification approaches addressed dense networks' weights or model predictions but did not formalize how mask structure, mask modification, training with/without triggers, fidelity thresholds, or ambiguity/inversion capacity should be composed into a verification protocol for sparse tickets. Without such a framework, design choices (e.g., whether to rely on mask inspection or trigger sets, how to define matching thresholds $\epsilon_f,\epsilon_s$, and how to reason about invertibility attacks) remained informal and scattered, impeding principled method design and evaluation targeted to the special properties of winning tickets.

Reasoning about ownership tied to sparse masks requires formal, unambiguous definitions so that (a) what it means for a mask to be a "winning ticket" can be tested quantitatively, (b) comparisons between masks (e.g., how much sparser one mask is than another) are well-defined, and (c) the notion of an "extremely sparse" ticket (one that cannot be pruned further without performance loss) is made precise. Prior work on the lottery ticket hypothesis provided informal concepts but not this compact set of formulas and the extreme-ticket criterion needed to ground ownership-verification protocols and security analyses.

Protecting an untrained sparse mask by distributing a small key instead of the full mask requires a principled way to select which subset of the mask should be withheld (the key) so that (i) the key is as small as possible for storage/distribution efficiency, and (ii) without the key the recipient cannot reconstruct a correct mask that trains to the expected performance. Prior ownership techniques did not provide a mask-subsetting procedure tailored to winning tickets' topology; therefore a concrete splitting algorithm with tunable relative-sparsity $n_s$ and multiple score heuristics was needed to operationalize the "lock-and-key" protection idea for masks.

Owners require a self-verifiable trained ticket that does not demand external key storage by users and is extractable from the sparse mask itself. Prior weight- or prediction-based watermarks either required weight-regularization (which changes training) or trigger sets (which are black-box only), and they did not exploit sparse mask topology. Embedding a binary signature directly into mask topology demands a method to generate a compact binary pattern, select embedding locations that are unlikely to be pruned away, and perform dimension-fitting when channel/kernel shapes differ — requirements which motivated the QR-code based encode function and the layer-selection and fitting procedure of Algorithm 2.

A practical ownership-protection solution for winning tickets must support realistic deployment modes: some consumers may only have black-box access (served APIs), others white-box access; some owners may accept distributing small keys, others prefer self-contained models. Existing watermarking methods did not provide a unified set of schemes that explicitly exploit mask structure and span this white-box/black-box design space with clear operational procedures and trade-offs. Hence it was necessary to define specific schemes (V1,V2,V3) that are implementable for winning tickets and to clarify their different threat models and usability costs.

It is necessary not only to propose protection schemes but to show they work empirically on realistic networks and datasets and that owner-specific credentials embedded in mask topology survive normal operations and deliberate attacks. Prior claims about mask importance were qualitative; what was missing was quantitative evidence that (a) extreme tickets can be found with very low remaining weights while matching dense accuracy, (b) embedding procedures minimally hurt accuracy, and (c) verification signals (performance gaps, decoded signatures, trigger accuracies) remain discriminative under reasonable perturbations. The experiments reported (Tables 1–3 and Fig. 2) fill this empirical gap.

Mask-based verification schemes are uniquely vulnerable to an attacker that selectively adds back small-magnitude weights in pruned positions to alter binary patterns (an attack that does not exist for dense-watermark schemes). Prior defenses designed for weight-space or prediction-space watermarks do not directly address this mask-specific threat. Therefore an explicit definition of add-on attacks and a simple owner-aware detection rule (prune-by-threshold $t$ known to the owner) plus empirical characterization of acceptable add-on rates were required to understand and bound this new attack vector.

If winning tickets are already dataset- and initialization-specific, owners might be able to demonstrate provenance even without explicit watermarking; however, this claim needed empirical substantiation so one can quantify how much fine-tuning or transfer undermines a purported match. Prior to this work, the connection between extreme-ticket mask specificity and its resistance to transfer/fine-tuning attacks as a practical verification signal had not been experimentally documented at the scale of modern conv-nets.

Embedding a binary signature into mask topology is useful only if the signature survives common model-space transformations, notably further pruning. Before proposing QR-based embedding, it was unknown empirically whether QR-like patterns could be embedded compactly enough and still be decodable under realistic post-distribution pruning attacks. Quantifying the pruning thresholds at which signatures remain decodable and when they are destroyed is essential for establishing practical security margins for mask-embedded credentials.

A formal ownership verification framework for extremely sparse winning tickets is defined as the tuple $\mathcal{V}=(ME,WE,F,V,I)$, where: $ME(\mathbf{M}_0,\mathbf{s})$ is an optional mask embedding process that takes an initial sparse mask $\mathbf{M}_0$ and an optional signature string $\mathbf{s}$ and outputs a modified mask $\mathbf{M}$ for mask-based verification; $WE(\mathbf{D}_{tr},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{s},\mathbb{N}[\cdot],L,\mathbf{W}_0,\mathbf{M})$ is the weight-embedding (training) process that returns a trained network $\mathbb{N}$ with sparse weights $\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}$, possibly embedding a trigger set $\mathbf{T}$ and/or signature $\mathbf{s}$; $F(\mathbb{N}[\cdot],\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M},\mathbf{D}_{te},\mathcal{A}_f,\epsilon_f)$ evaluates fidelity by checking $|\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}],\mathbf{D}_{te})-\mathcal{A}_f|<\epsilon_f$; $V(\mathbb{N}[\cdot],\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{s},\epsilon_s)$ performs verification either by inspecting $\mathbf{M}$ (white-box) or checking trigger-set predictions (black-box) with threshold $\epsilon_s$; and $I(\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}],\mathbf{T},\mathbf{s})$ denotes an invertibility/ambiguity attack procedure if one can reverse-engineer forged $(\mathbf{T}',\mathbf{s}',\mathbf{M}')$ that still verify and satisfy the fidelity test. This formalization operationalizes ownership verification specifically for sparse masks, specifies white-box and black-box verification primitives, and makes the security goal (resistance to removal and ambiguity attacks) explicit.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified; the framework's formal structure is internally consistent and the explicit inclusion of the invert process I (H8) provides a principled treatment of ambiguity attacks. The conclusion that a formal verification framework is defined is strongly supported within its stated scope as a conceptual foundation.

nodes.title: Formal verification framework for extremely sparse winning tickets

nodes.content: A subnetwork is defined as $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}]=\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}](\cdot)$ where $\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{\text{shape}(\mathbf{W})}$ is a binary mask. Sparsity of a mask $\mathbf{M}$ is $\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M}):=\|\mathbf{M}\|_0/\|\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{1}\|_0$ where $\|\cdot\|_0$ counts non-zero entries and $\mathbf{1}$ is a matrix of ones of the same shape. Relative sparsity is $\operatorname{rspar}(\mathbf{M}_1,\mathbf{M}_2):=\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M}_1)/(\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M}_2)+\epsilon)$, with $\epsilon$ a small positive constant to avoid division by zero. A winning ticket is a subnetwork $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_0,\mathbf{M}]$ (with $\mathbf{W}_0$ the network's initialization) that, when retrained, achieves test accuracy within 1% (a predefined threshold) of the dense model $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_0]$'s test accuracy. An extremely sparse winning ticket $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_0,\mathbf{M}_e]$ is a winning ticket such that increasing the sparsity of $\mathbf{M}_e$ by a factor $t$ (sparsity-difference threshold; experimentally $t=0.01$) yields a subnetwork that is no longer a winning ticket.

metadata.narrative: Precise definitions of subnetworks, sparsity, and extreme tickets are presented, but P1 reveals a gap between the formal extreme condition (threshold $t=0.01$) and the heuristic pruning schedule used to find tickets; the empirical operation does not directly verify the condition. No highlight offsets this gap, so the claim of "precise definitions" is only partially met in practice because the operationalisation does not enforce the definition.

nodes.title: Formal definitions of subnetwork, sparsity, relative sparsity, and extremely sparse winning ticket condition

nodes.content: An algorithm splits the mask $\{\mathbf{M}_l\}_{l=1}^N$ of an extremely sparse winning ticket into key masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l^s\}_{l=1}^N$ and locked masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l-\mathbf{M}_l^s\}_{l=1}^N$: given the initialization weights $\{\mathbf{W}_l\}_{l=1}^N$, score matrices $\{\mathbf{S}_l\}$ are computed from $\{\mathbf{W}_l\odot\mathbf{M}_l\}$ using a chosen score function, scores at positions already pruned (where $\mathbf{M}_l$ entries are zero) are set to $-\infty$, the threshold $T$ is the $n^{\text{th}}$ largest score across all layers ($n$ controls total non-zero elements in the key masks), and $\mathbf{M}_l^s$ is set element-wise as $\mathbb{I}_{\mathbf{S}_l>T}$. Supported scoring functions include One-Shot Magnitude (OMP: absolute weight values), Edge-Weight-Product (EWP: product of weights along input–output paths), edge betweenness centrality (Betweenness), and random scoring.

metadata.narrative: The mask splitting algorithm is validated across multiple scoring functions and datasets (H1), demonstrating that the lock-and-key concept is robust and not dependent on a particular heuristic. No load-bearing weak points were identified; the derivation is well-supported by the empirical evidence.

nodes.title: Mask splitting algorithm for creating key masks and supported scoring functions

nodes.content: A mask-embedding method embeds an owner-specific binary signature $\mathbf{s}$ into the sparse masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l\}$ of an extremely sparse winning ticket. The method generates a binary signature mask $\mathbf{M}_s = \text{encode}(\mathbf{s})$ (chosen implementation: QR code without finder, alignment, or version patterns), squeezes each layer mask $\mathbf{M}_l$ to a 2-D binary projection $\mathbf{M}_l^f$ via $(\mathbf{M}_l^f)_{ij} = \mathbb{I}_{\|(\mathbf{M}_l)_{ij}\|_0 > 0}$, locates the layer $l$ with maximal 0-1 similarity between $\mathbf{M}_l^f$ and $\mathbf{M}_s$ (call it $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$), and fits a resized $\mathbf{M}_s$ into the most similar region of $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$ (using random connections to expand to higher dimensions if needed) to produce embedded masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l^e\}$. The QR-code choice leverages its compact binary representation and error correction capability (e.g., H-level correction tolerating ~30% of errors) and the empirical observation that low-level convolutional layers are less sparse and therefore more robust locations for embedding.

metadata.narrative: The signature-embedding method shows strong empirical performance with minimal accuracy degradation and benefits from QR error correction (H2). However, P2 points out that the dimensionality expansion step for conv-layer masks is underspecified ("random connections"), hampering reproducibility. The highlight does not resolve this specification gap; the residual risk is that the implementation details may be non-trivial and the results may not be fully replicable.

nodes.title: Signature-embedding into sparse masks using QR-like encode function

nodes.content: Three concrete verification schemes are proposed and specified: (V1) split the mask of an extremely sparse winning ticket (extreme ticket) into locked and key masks; the owner distributes both (or distributes the locked mask and provides the key mask to legitimate users); verification occurs by merging the masks, retraining, and checking whether the performance drop when an incorrect key is used exceeds a threshold. (V2) embed a signature mask $\mathbf{M}_s$, generated by encoding an owner-specific binary signature string $\mathbf{s}$ into a binary matrix (e.g., a QR code pattern), into the extreme-ticket masks; ownership is verified in a white-box setting by extracting and decoding $\mathbf{M}_s$ from the trained sparse mask. (V3) combine the signature embedding of V2 with a trigger set $\mathbf{T}$ (a set of images and labels known to the owner) during retraining, so that verification can first proceed in black-box by evaluating the model's predictions on $\mathbf{T}$, and then escalate to white-box mask inspection if needed. Each scheme trades off user burden, deployment convenience, and verification access assumptions: V1 requires key handling, V2 requires white-box access, V3 enables black-box detection with optional white-box confirmation.

metadata.narrative: Three verification schemes are clearly described with operational procedures and trade-offs. No load-bearing weak points were identified in the scheme specifications themselves; their empirical validation is covered separately under conclusion 6. The derivation is competent but does not contain a distinguishing strength beyond the clear description.

nodes.title: Three verification schemes tailored to winning tickets: V1 (key masks), V2 (embedded signature white-box), V3 (embedded signature + trigger set black-box)

nodes.content: Extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that the proposed schemes are effective and robust on multiple architectures (ResNet-20, ResNet-18, ResNet-50) and benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100). Extremely sparse winning tickets achieve accuracies such as 91.66% on ResNet-20 CIFAR-10 with 19.369% remaining weights (dense model 91.67%). Embedding QR signatures causes minor performance drops: e.g., ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 achieves 91.37% (a 0.29% drop from the extreme accuracy of 91.66%); ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 achieves 93.56% (a 0.11% drop from its extreme accuracy of 93.60%). Combining embedding with trigger sets yields high trigger-set detection rates while preserving main-task accuracy: for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, trigger-set detection rate of 91.0% with a 0.20% main-task accuracy drop (from 91.66% to 91.46%). Retraining without the correct key mask causes large performance degradation, confirming the lock-and-key protection mechanism.

metadata.narrative: The empirical validation is extensive across architectures (ResNet-20/18/50, VGG-16) and datasets (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, Tiny-ImageNet) and covers multiple attack types (H3, H4), supporting claims of effectiveness and robustness. However, P3 (single-trial design without error bars) and P4 (heuristic extreme ticket discovery not matching the formal condition) introduce statistical uncertainty and a potential mismatch between experimental tickets and the theoretical definition. The highlights do not directly address these statistical and definitional gaps, so the numerical results should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

nodes.title: Empirical validation: effectiveness and robustness across architectures and datasets

nodes.content: A new attack class, called add-on attacks, is identified: attackers add small-magnitude noise to pruned weight positions to alter the sparse topology and create ambiguity for mask-based verification. A practical defense pipeline is proposed: the owner prunes weights whose magnitudes are below a threshold $t$ (known to the owner because the owner has the original mask) to detect suspicious additions. Empirical results show that add-on rates of 0.5% or less retain the matching condition (accuracy drop < 1%) and the QR code remains decodable; at 1% the matching criterion is violated (accuracy drop exceeds 1%) while the QR code is still decodable; at rates of 2% and above, both matching and decodeability fail, and test accuracy degrades sharply (e.g., at 2% test accuracy 86.64%, at 5% 79.49%, at 10% 71.06% for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10). This indicates detectability and a trade-off for attackers between masking credentials and preserving model utility.

metadata.narrative: The identification and characterization of add-on attacks (H5) provide a valuable new threat model and demonstrate that detection via performance drop or QR decode failure is feasible. However, the proposed defense pipeline (owner-prioritized magnitude pruning) is not actually evaluated in the experiments (P5), and the evaluation does not consider adaptive adversaries that fine-tune after adding weights (P6). The highlight does not cover these gaps; the conclusion that a practical defense pipeline exists is only partially supported by the available evidence.

nodes.title: Identification of add-on attacks and a practical detection/defense pipeline

nodes.content: Empirical evidence shows that extremely sparse winning tickets are intrinsically robust to fine-tuning and limited pruning, connecting mask topology tightly to the dataset and initialization. For example, transferring locked masks (with 5% key sparsity) found on CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100 yields test accuracy around 59.80% (OMP), while the extreme ticket found on CIFAR-100 achieves 66.39%, a gap exceeding 3%; similarly, transferring from CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10 yields 87.66% vs 91.66%. Trigger-based verification (Scheme V3) maintains detection rates above 89% under 5% pruning while main accuracy drops by less than 1%. Thus, even without deliberately embedding credentials, an extremely sparse winning ticket's unique mask structure can partly serve as a provenance signal for ownership.

metadata.narrative: Transfer experiments (H6) show consistent >3% performance gaps between CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, supporting the claim that the sparse mask is tied to the training dataset. However, P7 notes that these two datasets are similar; the experiment does not test more diverse dataset pairs or different initializations, limiting the generalizability of the "partial ownership signal" claim. The highlight is strong for the tested regime but the extrapolation beyond it remains uncertain.

nodes.title: Extreme tickets' intrinsic robustness to fine-tuning and pruning supports partial ownership claims

nodes.content: Binary signature masks embedded using the QR-code encode approach can be reliably decoded from trained sparse masks after realistic pruning attacks. For ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, the QR code remains decodable up to 20% one-shot magnitude pruning (decoded as readable string 'sigiature'), with test accuracy 88.03%. For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, the QR code is fully decodable at 5% pruning and partially decodable at 10% pruning (decoded as garbled string 'simçi@5re' at 10%). The decodability threshold varies by architecture.

metadata.narrative: The QR-code signature demonstrates notable robustness on ResNet-20 (H7), remaining decodable after 20% pruning. However, P8 shows that on ResNet-18 at 10% pruning the decoded output is garbled, indicating architecture-dependent robustness. P9 further highlights that only a single QR configuration was tested, so the generality across signature sizes and error correction levels is unknown. The highlight does not offset these architectural and configurational gaps; the claim of decodability under practical pruning levels is only conditionally supported.

nodes.title: QR-code style signatures embedded in masks remain decodable under practical pruning levels

nodes.content: The pruning schedule used to find extremely sparse winning tickets for ResNet-20 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 consists of iterative steps with fixed sparsity ratios (20%, 10%, 5%, 10% in that order) applied to the trained weights, stopping when further pruning degrades accuracy below the dense model's performance. The resulting mask sparsity is not directly compared to the formal extreme condition's threshold $t=0.01$ (i.e., it is not tested whether increasing the mask's sparsity by 1% relative to its current sparsity would preserve the winning ticket property).

metadata.failure_mode: If the heuristic schedule finds tickets that are not truly extreme (meaning they could be pruned another 1% without losing winning-ticket performance), then the foundation for the verification schemes is weaker: the extreme condition is often invoked to argue that the mask cannot be pruned further (e.g., for robustness claims), and the empirical results (Table 1) might not correspond to the paper's own definition. The conclusion that precise definitions are introduced becomes partially hollow because the operationalisation does not enforce the definition.
metadata.weakness_reason: The heuristic pruning schedule is a common practical approach but does not operationalize the formal definition: the condition "cannot be further pruned by $t \times 100\%$" requires a controlled sparsity increment of exactly 1%, not a sequence of larger jumps. The paper does not perform a finer-grained verification, so the discovered tickets may not actually be extreme in the defined sense. This disconnect is a measurement issue (what is measured vs what is defined) and a model assumption (the schedule is taken as sufficient).

nodes.title: Extreme ticket condition threshold not verified in pruning schedule

nodes.content: The mask embedding procedure takes a signature mask $\mathbf{M}_s$ (a 2D binary matrix produced by QR encoding) and fits it into the 2D projection $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$ of a convolutional-layer mask (4D tensor for conv layers). For masks with dimension higher than two, the step 'Change the dimension of $\mathbf{M}_s$ and fit it into $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$' is described only as using 'random connections' without any further specification of how the 2D pattern is expanded to the higher-dimensional mask (e.g., whether each channel receives a copy, a random subset, or another mapping). This lack of algorithmic detail leaves the expansion mechanism not fully specified.

metadata.failure_mode: If the dimensionality expansion is not precisely specified, the signature-embedding method cannot be reliably implemented by other researchers, and the results of Table 2 may depend on undocumented implementation details. The conclusion that Algorithm 2 provides a working embedding method is thus only weakly substantiated; the specific failure mode is that the method may not be reproducible or that "random connections" may degrade performance or decodeability in ways not captured in the paper's single implementation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper provides only a vague description of a critical step: embedding a 2D pattern into a 4D or higher-dimensional mask. Without precise specification, the method is not reproducible, which undermines the scientific contribution. Moreover, the choice of "random connections" could affect embedding fidelity and robustness, but no analysis or validation of that choice is given.

nodes.title: Insufficient specification of dimensionality expansion in mask embedding procedure

nodes.content: All reported experimental results are based on a single run per configuration, with no reported confidence intervals, standard deviations, or multiple seeds. The results thus lack characterization of variability due to random initialization, training stochasticity, and data partitioning.

metadata.failure_mode: If the single‑run results are not representative (i.e., the observed performance drops, detection rates, or robustness margins vary substantially across replications), then the quantitative claims about effectiveness and robustness — such as the precise accuracy drops in Tables 2 and 3, or the pruning thresholds at which signatures remain decodable — may not hold in general. The overall conclusion that the verification schemes are effective and robust would be materially weaker without statistical validation.
metadata.weakness_reason: Deep neural network training is known to exhibit non‑negligible variance across random seeds, and single‑trial results can be misleading, especially for small effect sizes (e.g., the 0.29% accuracy drop in Table 2). Without error bars, it is impossible to assess whether observed differences and robustness claims are statistically significant or within expected noise.

nodes.title: Experiments conducted with a single run per configuration and no error bars

nodes.content: The extremely sparse winning tickets used in the empirical evaluation of verification schemes are identified via a fixed iterative pruning schedule with ratios 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.1 and early stopping when accuracy drops. It is not tested whether any of these tickets can be further pruned by 0.01 in relative sparsity (the threshold $t$ defined in the extreme condition) without losing the winning ticket property. Therefore, these tickets may not satisfy the formal definition of an extremely sparse winning ticket, which could affect robustness claims that depend on extreme sparsity.

metadata.failure_mode: If the empirical tickets are not extreme, then the robustness claims (e.g., that pruning further at 20% still preserves signatures) might be artifacts of the specific pruning schedule and not general properties of the definition. The conclusion that the schemes are effective across the targeted regime would be undermined because the regime itself is not precisely defined.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same operationalisation gap as P1, but here it directly threatens the empirical foundation: all downstream experiments (effectiveness, robustness, signature embedding, etc.) rely on these tickets. If the tickets are not actually extreme, the observed performance and robustness might differ from what would be obtained with truly extreme tickets.

nodes.title: Empirical extreme tickets may not satisfy formal extreme condition

nodes.content: The proposed defense pipeline against add-on attacks consists of owner-prioritized detection: pruning weights whose magnitudes are below a threshold $t$ (known to the owner because the owner has the original mask). However, the reported experimental results do not implement this specific detection step. Instead, they use two indirect indicators: the 'Match?' condition (whether test accuracy drop is less than 1%) and the 'Decode-able?' condition (whether the QR code can still be decoded). The magnitude-pruning detection is not applied to the attacked models, so its practical effectiveness is not demonstrated.

metadata.failure_mode: If the magnitude-pruning detection pipeline is not validated, then the conclusion that a practical defense exists is unsupported; the only detection evidence shown is based on global performance drops and QR decode failure, which may be less precise or harder to apply in practice. The specific failure is that the claimed defense mechanism remains untested, so the security against add-on attacks is weaker than claimed.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper describes a specific detection method but does not test it; the experiments evaluate a different set of indicators (accuracy match and QR decode). This disconnect means that the claim "a practical defense pipeline is proposed" is not backed by evidence that the pipeline itself works. A reader cannot evaluate whether the threshold-based pruning detection would successfully identify added weights, nor at what false-positive/negative rates.

nodes.title: Owner-prioritized magnitude pruning detection not implemented in add-on attack experiments

nodes.content: The experimental evaluation of add-on attacks is conducted on the trained model after adding noise to pruned positions, without attacker adaptation such as fine-tuning after the add-on. Fine-tuning could change the magnitudes of the added weights, potentially reducing the effectiveness of threshold-based pruning detection that relies on magnitude separation. This adaptive scenario is not tested, so the defense's robustness under a more sophisticated threat model remains unknown.

metadata.failure_mode: If an attacker fine-tunes after add-on, the performance drop might be smaller (as the model adapts), and the threshold-based detection might fail because added weights' magnitudes become indistinguishable from original weights. In that case, the proposed defense would be ineffective, and the conclusion that the defense is practical would be invalidated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The evaluation only considers a static add-on attack where the attacker simply adds small noise. A reasonable attacker might attempt to fine-tune the model after adding weights to blend the added weights into the normal weight distribution. The paper's defense implicitly assumes that added weights remain separable by magnitude, which may not hold after fine-tuning.

nodes.title: Adaptive adversary not considered for add-on defense

nodes.content: The dataset-specificity claim is supported only by transfer experiments between CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. These two datasets are subsets of the same image collection with shared categories and similar image statistics. Transfer to substantially different datasets (e.g., to Tiny-ImageNet or ImageNet) or across different random initializations of the same architecture is not tested. Therefore, the generalization of the dataset-specificity claim is not established.

metadata.failure_mode: If dataset-specificity is weaker for diverse dataset pairs (e.g., CIFAR-10 to ImageNet), the claim that the mask structure can serve as a provenance signal becomes less credible; the partial ownership claim would be restricted to very similar datasets, reducing its practical value. The conclusion that intrinsic robustness supports ownership claims would be overgeneralized.
metadata.weakness_reason: The evidence for dataset-specificity rests on a single pair of similar datasets. The shared structure of CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (both are 32×32 natural images with similar classes) means that the performance gap might be larger when transferring to a more distant dataset, but the paper does not provide that evidence. Additionally, different random initializations of the same dataset could also yield distinct masks, which is not explored.

nodes.title: Dataset-specificity claims based on limited transfer experiments between CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, after 10% one-shot magnitude pruning, the QR code extracted decodes to the garbled string 'simçi@5re' rather than the embedded string 'signature', while for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 the same pruning ratio yields a fully decodable QR code. Thus, the claim that QR-code signatures remain decodable under practical pruning levels is not consistently supported across architectures; the decodability threshold varies.

metadata.failure_mode: If the signature is not reliably decodable on certain architectures at moderate pruning levels, then the conclusion that QR-code signatures remain decodable under practical pruning is false for a significant subset of models. Ownership verification via mask extraction would be unreliable for those architectures, weakening the overall contribution.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's main claim about decodability is stated in a sweeping manner, but the empirical evidence shows that on ResNet-18, even 10% pruning produces only partial decoding. Since ResNet-18 is a deeper architecture with different mask topology, the robustness of the embedding method appears architecture-dependent. The paper does not explain why the difference occurs or adjust the claim accordingly.

nodes.title: Decodability not uniform across architectures

nodes.content: In all experiments, the signature mask is generated with a single QR code configuration: H correction level (30% error tolerance) and unstated QR version (e.g., version 1 with 21×21 pixels is typical). The robustness of the embedded signature to pruning and additive noise is tested only for this single configuration. Different signature lengths or QR versions with different error correction capacities could affect decodability, so the generality of the observed robustness is not explored.

metadata.failure_mode: If a different QR configuration (e.g., shorter error correction or larger payload) were used, the decodability threshold might change, potentially reducing the claimed robustness. The conclusion that the method works across practical pruning levels would then be contingent on the particular QR setup, not a property of the embedding approach itself.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's robustness conclusions are based on one specific QR implementation. The choice of version and correction level directly affects the amount of redundancy. Without testing multiple configurations, it is unclear whether the decodability margins observed are general or highly specific to the chosen parameters.

nodes.title: QR configuration not varied

nodes.content: For ResNet-20 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the mask splitting algorithm (Algorithm 1) is evaluated with four different scoring functions—One-Shot Magnitude (OMP), Edge-Weight-Product (EWP), edge betweenness centrality, and random scoring—across a range of key mask relative sparsities (from 0% to about 20%). The resulting performance of re-training without key masks is consistently degraded, and the choice of scoring function does not alter the qualitative trend (Fig. 2).

metadata.credit: This validation preempts the failure mode that the lock-and-key effect might depend on a specific choice of scoring function; it underwrites the reliability of the splitting algorithm and supports the conclusion that the lock-and-key concept is robust across different heuristics, strengthening the claim that scheme V1 is generally effective.

nodes.title: Validation of key mask splitting across scoring functions

nodes.content: For ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, embedding a QR-code signature mask using Algorithm 2 results in a test accuracy of 91.37%, a drop of only 0.29% from the original extreme ticket's 91.66% (Table 2). The same small drop (0.11%) is observed for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10. The QR code uses the H error correction level, which can tolerate up to 30% of the code being erroneous.

metadata.credit: This strength directly preempts the risk that embedding a signature significantly degrades the winning ticket's performance, which would undermine the utility of scheme V2. The small empirical drops paired with the error-correction capability indicate that the embedding method is both low-disturbance and error-tolerant, supporting the conclusion that the signature-embedding method is effective and practical.

nodes.title: QR embedding preserves performance and provides error correction

nodes.content: The evaluation of the proposed verification schemes (V1, V2, V3) is conducted on three architectures—ResNet-20, ResNet-18, and ResNet-50—and four datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet (in Appendix A2), and Tiny-ImageNet (for VGG-16 in Appendix). The results show consistent patterns in terms of extreme ticket sparsity, embedding performance drops, and robustness to attacks across these settings.

metadata.credit: This breadth preempts the failure mode that the methods might only work on a single architecture/scale, which would severely limit the conclusion's claim of effectiveness. The multi-architecture and multi-dataset validation supports the generalization of the empirical conclusions to a wider range of models and tasks.

nodes.title: Empirical validation across multiple architectures and datasets

nodes.content: The paper evaluates all three verification schemes against a comprehensive set of attacks: fine-tuning (Table 4 and text), model pruning with multiple methods and ratios (Tables 5 and 6), add-on attacks with rates from 0% to 10% (Table 8, Fig 6), and three types of ambiguity attacks (fake1, fake2, fake3, Table 7, Fig 5). Quantitative metrics include test accuracy, trigger set detection accuracy, QR decode success, and match condition.

metadata.credit: This comprehensive attack evaluation preempts the failure mode that the schemes might be vulnerable to an unanticipated simple attack. The systematic coverage across removal and ambiguity attacks supports the conclusion that the methods are robust under a variety of adversarial manipulations, strengthening the security claims.

nodes.title: Comprehensive attack evaluation

nodes.content: Add-on attacks—where an attacker adds small-magnitude weights to pruned positions to alter the sparse mask—are systematically tested on ResNet-20 at rates from 0.5% to 10% (Table 8, Fig 6). The results show that at add-on rates up to 0.5%, the QR code remains decodable and the match condition is satisfied; at 1% the match condition fails but QR decoding still succeeds; at higher rates both fail and test accuracy degrades substantially (from 91.53% to 79.49% at 5% add-on).

metadata.credit: This characterization preempts the failure mode that add-on attacks might be completely undetectable. The quantitative trade-off between add-on rate, model utility, and verification signal demonstrates that the attack is detectable at moderate rates, supporting the conclusion that practical detection (via performance drop or QR decode failure) is feasible and that the attack is a real threat with specific boundaries.

nodes.title: Characterization of add-on attacks and detection trade-offs

nodes.content: For ResNet-20, transferring locked masks (obtained via OMP, EWP, Betweenness at 5% relative sparsity) from CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100 yields test accuracies of 59.80%, 60.27%, and 59.61% respectively, while the extreme ticket found directly on CIFAR-100 achieves 66.39%. Similarly, transferring CIFAR-100 masks to CIFAR-10 yields accuracies around 87.2–88.2% compared to the direct CIFAR-10 extreme ticket's 91.66%. These performance gaps exceed 3%, well above the 1% matching criterion.

metadata.credit: This quantitative evidence preempts the failure mode that the mask structure might be interchangeable across datasets. The large performance gaps support the conclusion that the sparse mask is intrinsically tied to the training dataset, providing a partial ownership signal even without explicit watermarking. The consistency across multiple scoring functions strengthens this claim.

nodes.title: Consistent transfer performance gaps support dataset specificity

nodes.content: For ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10, after one-shot magnitude pruning at 20% pruning ratio, the extracted QR code decodes to "sigiature" (a single-character error from the original "signature") and is considered decodable by the paper. The test accuracy at this pruning level is 88.03%, a drop of 3.34% from the original 91.37%. At 5% and 10% pruning, the code is fully decodable to "signature".

metadata.credit: This result preempts the failure mode that even moderate pruning would completely destroy the embedded signature. The demonstration that the QR code remains human-readable and essentially correct after 20% weight removal supports the conclusion that the embedded signature is robust under practically relevant pruning regimes for at least one major architecture (ResNet-20).

nodes.title: QR decodability demonstrated under significant pruning on ResNet-20

nodes.content: In the verification framework $\mathcal{V}$ defined as a tuple $(ME,WE,F,V,I)$, the invert process $I$ explicitly captures ambiguity attacks by stating conditions under which a forged signature, trigger set, or mask can still satisfy verification and fidelity tests. This formal component is absent from prior sparse-ownership work.

metadata.credit: This inclusion preempts the failure mode that the framework might ignore the possibility of attackers reverse-engineering verifiable credentials. By modeling the invert process, the framework operationalizes the security goal of resistance to ambiguity attacks, supporting the conclusion that the framework is comprehensive and tailored to the threat landscape of lottery ticket ownership.

nodes.title: Explicit modeling of ambiguity attacks via invert process I

steps.reasoning: Treat as known the formal mask and sparsity definitions: $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}]$, $\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{\text{shape}(\mathbf{W})}$, $\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M})$, $\operatorname{rspar}(\cdot,\cdot)$, and the extreme-ticket condition (the result of conclusion 2).

Define a verification framework as a tuple $\mathcal{V}=(ME,WE,F,V,I)$ where each component is a concrete process that participates in ownership verification for extremely sparse winning tickets; explicitly list the arguments and outputs for each process so that protocol behavior and success conditions are fully specified.

Specify the mask embedding process $ME$ and its signature argument: define $ME(\mathbf{M}_0,\mathbf{s})$ as a (possibly optional) procedure that takes an initial sparse mask $\mathbf{M}_0$ and an optional signature string $\mathbf{s}$ and returns a modified mask $\mathbf{M}$ which may have $\mathbf{s}$ embedded or other structural modifications useful for mask-based verification; label methods that use $ME$ as "mask-based".

Specify the weight-embedding (training) process $WE$ with its full inputs: define $WE(\mathbf{D}_{tr},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{s},\mathbb{N}[\cdot],L,\mathbf{W}_0,\mathbf{M})$ as the learning process that takes a training dataset $\mathbf{D}_{tr}=\{\mathbf{x},y\}$, an optional trigger set $\mathbf{T}=\{\mathbf{T}_x,\mathbf{T}_y\}$, an optional signature $\mathbf{s}$, a model architecture $\mathbb{N}[\cdot]$, a loss function $L$ (e.g., cross-entropy), an initialization $\mathbf{W}_0$, and a sparse mask $\mathbf{M}$, and returns a trained model $\mathbb{N}$ with sparse weights $\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}$ where $\mathbf{W}$ denotes the trained weights; note that $\mathbf{T}$ and/or $\mathbf{s}$ may be embedded into $\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}$ during this process.

Specify the fidelity evaluation process $F$ and its thresholding condition for acceptable performance: define $F(\mathbb{N}[\cdot],\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M},\mathbf{D}_{te},\mathcal{A}_f,\epsilon_f)$ to compute the model performance $\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}],\mathbf{D}_{te})$ on a test dataset $\mathbf{D}_{te}$ and assert that fidelity holds when the absolute difference $|\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}],\mathbf{D}_{te})-\mathcal{A}_f|<\epsilon_f$, where $\mathcal{A}_f$ is a target inference performance and $\epsilon_f$ is a pre-defined tolerance.

Specify the verification process $V$ that implements both mask-based (white-box) and trigger-based (black-box) checks: define $V(\mathbb{N}[\cdot],\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{s},\epsilon_s)$ to (a) in white-box/mask-based mode, inspect $\mathbf{M}$ and/or extract a signature $\mathbf{s}$ from $\mathbf{M}$ and/or check that evaluating $\mathbb{N}[\cdot,\mathbf{M}]$ on a validation set yields a performance gap below threshold $\epsilon_s$; and (b) in black-box/trigger-set mode, run inference on $\mathbf{T}_x$ and compare predictions against $\mathbf{T}_y$, declaring verification success if a trigger-set detection metric (e.g., false-detection rate) is below $\epsilon_s$.

Specify the invertibility/ambiguity attack process $I$ that captures forged-forgery threats: define $I(\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}],\mathbf{T},\mathbf{s})$ as an adversarial inversion or ambiguity attempt that is successful if an attacker can produce forged $(\mathbf{T}',\mathbf{s}',\mathbf{M}')$ that (a) can be reverse-engineered from $\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}$ or otherwise constructed, (b) pass the verification checks relative to the authentic model and mask, and (c) satisfy the fidelity evaluation $F(\mathbb{N}[\cdot],\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}',\mathbf{D}_{te},\mathcal{A}_t,\epsilon_f)$ so that the forged artifact remains performant.

Explain how this formalization operationalizes ownership verification for sparse masks: by explicitly listing the processes, inputs, outputs, and numeric thresholds ($\epsilon_f,\epsilon_s$) the framework makes concrete (a) mask-based versus trigger-based choices, (b) fidelity and verification acceptance criteria, and (c) the security goal of resistance to removal and ambiguity/inversion attacks, thereby filling the previously informal gap in prior verification literature for extremely sparse winning tickets.

Define a neural network parameterized by a weight tensor $\mathbf{W}$ as $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}](\cdot)$ where $\mathbb{N}$ denotes the model architecture and $\mathbf{W}$ denotes its weights; define a sparse mask $\mathbf{M}$ as a binary tensor with the same shape as $\mathbf{W}$, i.e., $\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{\text{shape}(\mathbf{W})}$; define a subnetwork of $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}]$ by applying element-wise multiplication of weights and mask as $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}]:=\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}\odot\mathbf{M}](\cdot)$ so that only entries where $(\mathbf{M})_{i}=1$ remain active.

Introduce a sparsity measure for a mask: define $\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M}):=\|\mathbf{M}\|_{0}/\|\mathbf{M}+1\|_{0}$ where $\|\cdot\|_{0}$ denotes the count of non-zero entries; this provides a scalar quantification of how sparse $\mathbf{M}$ is relative to its full shape.

Define relative sparsity between two masks to compare their sparsities: for two masks $\mathbf{M}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{2}$, define $\operatorname{rspar}(\mathbf{M}_{1},\mathbf{M}_{2}):=\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M}_{1})/(\operatorname{spar}(\mathbf{M}_{2})+\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon$ is a small constant added to the denominator to avoid division by zero; this gives a normalized ratio indicating how much sparser $\mathbf{M}_{1}$ is compared to $\mathbf{M}_{2}$.

Define the criterion for a winning ticket in this formalism: given an initialization $\mathbf{W}_{0}$, call $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_{0},\mathbf{M}]$ a winning ticket if, after retraining from initialization $\mathbf{W}_{0}$ using mask $\mathbf{M}$, the test performance of $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_{0},\mathbf{M}]$ matches that of the dense model $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_{0}]$ according to a chosen matching threshold (the authors suggest e.g., within $1\%$ absolute performance), thereby operationalizing the informal lottery-ticket hypothesis [1].
[1]

Formalize the "extremely sparse" (extreme-ticket) condition: given a sparsity-difference threshold $t$ (a scalar fraction), call $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_{0},\mathbf{M}_e]$ an extremely sparse winning ticket if (a) $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W}_{0},\mathbf{M}_e]$ can match the dense model performance under the winning-ticket matching criterion, and (b) increasing the sparsity of $\mathbf{M}_e$ further by a multiplicative factor of $t$ (i.e., pruning an additional $t\times 100\%$ of remaining weights) cannot produce another mask that still satisfies the winning-ticket matching criterion; in the experiments $t$ is set to $0.01$.

Justify the need for these precise definitions: ownership verification for sparse masks requires (a) a quantitative test for whether a mask is a winning ticket (the retraining-and-accuracy matching rule), (b) well-defined comparisons between masks (the $\operatorname{spar}$ and $\operatorname{rspar}$ formulas), and (c) a precise extreme-ticket criterion (the $t$-based non-prunability condition) so that later protocols and security analyses can unambiguously specify thresholds and success conditions.

Treat as known the mask and sparsity formalism: masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l\}_{l=1}^N$, weights $\{\mathbf{W}_l\}_{l=1}^N$, notion of relative sparsity $\operatorname{rspar}(\cdot,\cdot)$, and the goal of withholding a small key-mask subset so that without it the locked masks cannot retrain to match dense performance (result of conclusion 2).

State the protection objective and decision variables: given an extremely sparse ticket mask $\{\mathbf{M}_l\}_{l=1}^N$, seek key sub-masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l^s\}_{l=1}^N$ with as few non-zero elements as possible (minimizing storage/distribution cost) subject to the locked masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l-\mathbf{M}_l^s\}_{l=1}^N$ causing large performance degradation when used alone for retraining; control the relative sparsity of the key masks by a hyperparameter $n_s$ specifying $\operatorname{rspar}(\{\mathbf{M}_l^s\},\{\mathbf{M}_l\})<n_s$.

Describe algorithmic scoring and thresholding: compute score matrices $\{\mathbf{S}_l\}_{l=1}^N$ by applying a chosen score function $\text{score}(\cdot)$ to the masked weights $\{\mathbf{W}_l\odot\mathbf{M}_l\}_{l=1}^N$ where $\text{score}(\cdot)$ produces a scalar importance value for each weight entry; the scoring is performed layer-wise to produce $\mathbf{S}_l$ for each layer $l$.

Handle already-pruned positions by excluding them from key selection: set entries of $\mathbf{S}_l$ to negative infinity at positions where $(\mathbf{W}_l\odot\mathbf{M}_l)$ is zero (i.e., already pruned) so that they cannot be selected into the key masks.

Select the top-$n$ scored elements across all layers to form key masks: determine a global threshold $T$ defined as the $n^{\text{th}}$ largest value across all entries of $\{\mathbf{S}_l\}_{l=1}^N$ where $n$ controls the total number of non-zero elements desired in the key masks; then set each key-layer mask by element-wise thresholding $\mathbf{M}_l^s\leftarrow\mathbb{I}_{\mathbf{S}_l>T}$ (indicator that the score exceeds $T$).

List supported scoring heuristics and their definitions for use in the pipeline: (a) One-Shot Magnitude (OMP): score each weight by its absolute value $|\mathbf{W}_{l,ij}|$; (b) Edge-Weight-Product (EWP): score paths by the product of weights along input-output paths (a path-based importance measure previously described in the literature) [35]; (c) edge betweenness centrality (Betweenness): define an edge weight for convolutional layers as the sum of absolute values of kernel elements and compute betweenness centrality for graph edges to serve as importance scores; and (d) random scoring: assign random scores to elements as a baseline.
[35]

Present the full splitting pipeline succinctly as Algorithm 1: input masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l\}$, weights $\{\mathbf{W}_l\}$, desired number of non-zeros $n$, and a score function $\text{score}(\cdot)$; compute $\{\mathbf{S}_l\}$, set already-pruned positions in $\mathbf{S}_l$ to $-\infty$, compute threshold $T$ as the $n^{\text{th}}$ largest score across layers, and set $\mathbf{M}_l^s\leftarrow\mathbb{I}_{\mathbf{S}_l>T}$ to obtain key masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l^s\}$ and locked masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l-\mathbf{M}_l^s\}$.

Explain the practical rationale: splitting the sparse mask into a small key and a locked remainder provides a lock-and-key protection for untrained masks so that (i) the key is small for distribution/storage efficiency and (ii) without the key the recipient cannot reconstruct a correct mask that retrains to expected performance; the scoring options give flexible heuristics to find compact high-importance subsets.

Treat as known the mask formalism and the empirical observation that low-level convolutional layers tend to be less sparse (result of conclusion 2 and experimental observation stated in the paper), motivating embedding into low-level conv layers for robustness.

Define the signature generation function and its output: introduce $\text{encode}(\cdot)$ that maps a binary string signature $\mathbf{s}$ to a binary signature mask $\mathbf{M}_s\in\{0,1\}^{d_1\times d_2}$; choose $\text{encode}(\cdot)$ to produce a compact 0-1 pattern suitable for mask embedding (implementation choice: QR-code-like binary pattern without finder/alignment/version patterns).
[36]

Describe squeezing layer masks to a 2-D binary projection for pattern matching: for each layer mask $\mathbf{M}_l$ (which may be multi-dimensional, e.g., channel/kernel dimensions), compute a two-dimensional projection $\mathbf{M}_l^f$ by setting $(\mathbf{M}_l^f)_{ij}=\mathbb{I}_{\|(\mathbf{M}_l)_{ij}\|_0>0}$ where $\|(\mathbf{M}_l)_{ij}\|_0$ counts non-zero entries along the collapsed dimensions, so that $\mathbf{M}_l^f$ records presence/absence (0/1) in spatial/channel positions and is comparable to $\mathbf{M}_s$.

Select an embedding location by 0–1 similarity: compute the percentage similarity (fraction of matching 0/1 entries) between each $\mathbf{M}_l^f$ and the signature mask $\mathbf{M}_s$, pick the layer projection with maximal similarity as $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$, and plan to fit a resized $\mathbf{M}_s$ into the most similar region of $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$ to minimize changes to $\mathbf{M}$.

Handle dimensional mismatches when fitting $\mathbf{M}_s$ into higher-dimensional masks: if a target $\mathbf{M}_l$ has more than two dimensions (e.g., extra channels), increase the dimension of $\mathbf{M}_s$ by random-channel expansion (random connections across channels) so the binary pattern can be embedded without introducing regular, easily-detectable artifacts; for strictly 2-D masks, directly replace the chosen region with $\mathbf{M}_s$.

Explain the QR-code choice and its practical advantages: select QR-code style binary encoding because (a) QR codes are naturally 0-1 patterns; (b) QR codes support error correction (e.g., H-level can tolerate up to $\sim30\%$ errors), increasing resilience to subsequent pruning/noise; (c) QR codes can be compact (minimum $21\times21$) which fits into convolutional layer channel/kernel dimensions; and (d) removing finder/alignment/version patterns makes embedded QR-like patterns less visually regular and therefore less conspicuous in masks.
[36]

Summarize the embedding pipeline as Algorithm 2: compute $\mathbf{M}_s\leftarrow\text{encode}(\mathbf{s})$, compute projections $\mathbf{M}_l^f$ by squeezing $\mathbf{M}_l$, find $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$ with highest similarity to $\mathbf{M}_s$, and change the dimension/fit $\mathbf{M}_s$ into the region of $\mathbf{M}_{max}^f$ with maximal similarity to produce embedded masks $\{\mathbf{M}_l^e\}_{l=1}^N$.

Treat as known the mask-splitting algorithm that produces key and locked masks (conclusion 3) and the signature-embedding procedure that produces embedded masks (conclusion 4); use these building blocks to construct concrete verification schemes.

Describe Scheme V1 (key masks): split an extreme-ticket mask $\mathbf{M}$ into locked masks $\mathbf{M}_l$ and small key masks $\mathbf{M}_s$ (as per Algorithm 1); distribute either both parts to legitimate users or distribute locked masks and give the key to authorized users; require legitimate users to merge locked and key masks (element-wise addition of masked weights or mask union) and retrain the model from the prescribed initialization $\mathbf{W}_0$; verify ownership by observing that incorrect or missing key masks produce degraded retraining fidelity (performance drops) relative to the fidelity threshold $\epsilon_f$.

Describe Scheme V2 (embedded signature, white-box): apply Algorithm 2 to embed a signature mask $\mathbf{M}_s$ into the extreme-ticket masks, train the model so the embedded signature is present in the distributed sparse model $\mathbb{N}[\mathbf{W},\mathbf{M}]$, and perform verification in the white-box setting by extracting $\mathbf{M}_s$ from the recipient's sparse mask and decoding it back to the owner-specific signature string $\mathbf{s}$; this requires direct access to the model weights/masks.

Describe Scheme V3 (embedded signature + trigger set, black-box capable): combine Scheme V2's mask-embedded signature with training on a trigger set $\mathbf{T}$ (a set of input-label pairs used solely for verification); during distributed use the owner can perform black-box verification by querying the model API with $\mathbf{T}_x$ and checking predicted labels against $\mathbf{T}_y$ to detect an elevated trigger-set accuracy or detection rate; if black-box probing raises a red flag, escalate to white-box examination of the mask to decode $\mathbf{M}_s$ as in Scheme V2.

Characterize trade-offs: Scheme V1 requires explicit key handling and thus imposes storage/distribution/user burden but allows mask-protection without embedding; Scheme V2 is user-friendly (self-contained model) but requires white-box access for verification; Scheme V3 enables initial black-box detection (suitable for API-served models) and optional white-box confirmation, trading off some training complexity (trigger-set insertion) for broader verification modalities.

Explain operational validation: each scheme has a clear operational procedure (preprocess/ticket finding/training/inference/validation) so that owners can choose the scheme that matches their deployment constraints (key management vs. white-box access vs. black-box probing) and threat models.

Treat as given the three verification schemes V1, V2, V3 (conclusion 5) and the Algorithms 1 and 2 used to prepare protected tickets; now validate these schemes empirically across specified architectures and datasets.

State experimental scope and setup concisely: experiments were run on multiple architectures (ResNet-20, ResNet-18, ResNet-50) and datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) using the described train/retrain protocol (SGD optimizer with momentum, specified weight decays, 182 epochs with scheduled learning-rate drops and late rewinding to the 3rd checkpoint) to identify extremely sparse winning tickets and to measure verification robustness.

Report representative extreme-ticket quantitative results from the reported summary: from the performance/pruning summary (Table 1), for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 the dense-model accuracy is $91.67\%$ and the extreme-ticket accuracy is $91.66\%$ with $19.369\%$ of weights remaining (pruning specification reported in Table 1), illustrating that extremely sparse tickets can match dense performance at low remaining-weight proportions.
Table 1

Report the effect of QR-signature embedding (Scheme V2) on main-task accuracy using the reported numbers: from Table 2, embedding QR signatures causes only minor performance drops — ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 yields $91.37\%$ after embedding (a $0.29\%$ drop), and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 yields $93.56\%$ after embedding (a $0.11\%$ drop) — showing embedding is low-cost in accuracy.
Table 2

Report trigger-set results for Scheme V3 demonstrating high trigger detection while preserving main accuracy: from Table 3, for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 using extremely sparse winning tickets with embedded signature plus trigger set, main-task accuracy is $91.46\%$ (a $0.20\%$ drop from $91.66\%$) while trigger-set detection rate is $91.0\%$, showing trigger-based black-box detection can be effective with minimal main-task impact.
Table 3

Report Scheme V1 empirical validation that wrong or missing keys cause large retraining degradation: retraining experiments without key masks (Figure 2) show that increasing numbers of '1's withheld in the key mask (i.e., larger relative sparsity of the missing key) lead to larger performance divergence after retraining; this validates the lock-and-key protection idea in practice by demonstrating that incorrect/missing keys substantially harm retrained accuracy.
Fig. 2

Conclude empirical effectiveness and robustness: the reported experiments across architectures and datasets demonstrate (a) extreme tickets with very low remaining-weight proportions can match dense accuracy, (b) QR-like embedding imposes only minor accuracy penalties, and (c) verification signals (retraining performance gaps, decoded signatures, trigger-set detection rates) remain discriminative under reasonable manipulations, thereby empirically validating the proposed schemes.
Table 1
Table 2; Table 3; Fig. 2
Treat as known the verification schemes (conclusion 5) and empirical validation (conclusion 6); focus now on a newly identified threat vector that specifically targets mask-based verification.

Define the add-on attack class and attacker capability: an add-on attack is one where an attacker attempts to "recover" some pruned positions by adding small-magnitude weights (noise) at previously pruned positions in the sparse mask, thereby changing the binary sparsity topology of $\mathbf{M}$ while attempting to preserve model utility; define "add-on rate" as the fraction (percentage) of pruned positions that are reactivated with small-magnitude noise.

Propose a simple, owner-prioritized detection/defense pipeline: the owner, who knows the authentic pruning threshold $t$ (a magnitude threshold used when pruning), can detect suspicious additions by re-pruning weights whose magnitudes are below $t$; this prune-by-threshold removes small-magnitude additions and reveals whether an attacker has injected add-on noise that is detectable relative to the known owner threshold $t$.

Report empirical characterization of add-on attack effects and detection trade-offs from experiments: Table 8 reports test accuracy and remaining-weight proportion after add-on attacks at various add-on rates on ResNet-20, and Fig. 6 visualizes extracted QR codes post-add-on; specifically, for add-on rate $0\%$ the test accuracy is $91.53\%$ with remaining-weight $19.369\%$, QR decodable (✓), match (✓); for $0.5\%$ the accuracy is $91.04\%$ ($19.789\%$), QR decodable (✓), match (✓); for $1\%$ the accuracy is $90.23\%$ ($20.179\%$), QR decodable (✓) but match fails (✗); for $2\%$ the accuracy is $86.64\%$ ($21.009\%$) with QR not decodable (✗) and match fails (✗); larger rates further degrade accuracy and decodability (see Table 8).
Table 8; Fig. 6

Interpret the empirical findings as a detectability trade-off: small add-on rates (≤0.5%) allow the QR signature to remain decodable and the match criterion to hold, making weak add-on attacks unsuccessful at creating ambiguity; modest add-on rates around 1% can break the matching criterion (so a forged model will fail verification) while still leaving QR decodable, and larger add-on rates both destroy decodability and substantially reduce test accuracy, indicating attackers face a trade-off between masking credentials and preserving model utility, and that owner-aware threshold-repruning can detect suspicious add-ons.

Start from the empirical validation baseline (conclusion 6) showing extreme tickets and verification schemes work, and analyze how intrinsic properties of extreme tickets support partial ownership claims without explicit embedding.

State the experimental transfer/fine-tuning setup used to probe intrinsic specificity: transfer locked masks identified on one dataset (e.g., CIFAR-10) to retraining on another dataset (e.g., CIFAR-100) and measure resulting test accuracy; the intent is to see whether masquerading by fine-tuning or dataset transfer can bypass the need for keys or signatures.

Report empirical transfer results demonstrating dataset-specificity of locked masks: Table 4 shows transferring ResNet-20 locked masks from CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100 (denoted $10\rightarrow100$) yields test accuracies such as $59.80\%$ (OMP 5% key-mask relative sparsity), and transferring from CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10 ($100\rightarrow10$) yields $87.66\%$ for the same OMP 5% case; these results produce performance gaps greater than $3\%$ relative to the original extreme-ticket accuracies (which are much higher for native-data tickets), exceeding the $1\%$ matching criterion and showing transferred locked masks do not reproduce the owner's winning-ticket performance.
Table 4

Report trigger/pruning robustness results relevant to partial claims: Table 5 shows that trigger-based verification (Scheme V3) maintains high trigger-set detection under modest pruning while main accuracy remains high — e.g., for ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 the original ESWT with embedding and trigger achieves $91.46\%$ main accuracy and $91.0\%$ trigger accuracy, pruning 5% yields $91.33\%$ main and $89.0\%$ trigger, pruning 10% yields $90.66\%$ main and $90.0\%$ trigger — indicating the sparse mask and trigger coupling persist under limited removal attacks.
Table 5

Synthesize the implications: because extreme tickets are tightly connected to their dataset and initialization, locked-mask transfers or fine-tuning do not recover the same performance, and trigger-based detection remains functional under modest pruning; therefore even absent explicit embedded credentials, an extremely sparse winning ticket's unique mask topology and dataset-specific retraining behavior can partially serve as a provenance signal for ownership claims.

Begin from the empirical evaluation of pruning robustness reported in the experiments (conclusion 6) and the QR-based embedding procedure (conclusion 4); focus on measuring the decodability of QR-like signatures after further pruning attacks.

Explain pruning methods and evaluation metrics used: pruning methods include one-shot magnitude pruning (OMP) and random pruning; pruning ratios denote the additional proportion of weights removed from the trained sparse model; decodability is assessed by extracting the embedded binary pattern from the mask after pruning and attempting to decode it back to the original signature string (readability/partial readability reported).

Report ResNet-20 OMP pruning resilience: Table 6 reports for Scheme V2 (QR-embedded) that after OMP $5\%$ pruning the CIFAR-10 accuracy is $91.25\%$, after OMP $10\%$ accuracy is $90.72\%$, and after OMP $20\%$ accuracy is $88.03\%$; the extracted QR code from ResNet-20 remains decodable up to $20\%$ one-shot magnitude pruning (Figure 3 shows that under 5% and 10% the code decodes to "signature" and under 20% decodes to a slightly corrupted string "sigiature"), demonstrating that QR-like signatures embedded in masks can survive realistic pruning levels while main-task accuracy degrades only gradually.
Table 6; Fig. 3

Report ResNet-18 pruning resilience and partial decodability: Figure 4 shows that for ResNet-18 the QR string extracted after $5\%$ pruning can be decoded to the readable string "signature", after $10\%$ pruning the string is partially decodable (e.g., noisy characters "simçi@5re"), and for pruning ratios greater than $10\%$ the main-task accuracy has already significantly dropped making further attack analysis less meaningful; Table 6 corroborates the accuracy drops for ResNet-18 under OMP and random pruning.
Fig. 4; Table 6

Conclude practical decodability bounds: empirically, QR-like binary signatures embedded into sparse masks can be reliably decoded after realistic pruning attacks — ResNet-20 QR remains readable under up to $20\%$ OMP pruning and ResNet-18 QR is decodable at $5\%$ and partially decodable at $10\%$ — providing concrete pruning-vs-decodability trade-offs useful for setting robustness margins for mask-embedded credentials.
Table 6; Fig. 3; Fig. 4

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges several remaining practical and empirical issues that require further work: (1) statistical reproducibility and uncertainty quantification — experiments were run as single trials due to resource limits and the authors explicitly commit to repeating experiments and reporting error bars to characterize variability across random seeds and runs; (2) operational costs and usability trade-offs of Scheme V1 — splitting and distributing key masks imposes storage, handling, and recovery responsibilities on legitimate users and the exact best trade-off between key size and security remains to be optimized; (3) white-box limitation and black-box trade-offs — Scheme V2 requires white-box weight access for mask extraction, and while Scheme V3 adds a trigger-set to enable black-box verification, the design of trigger sets that maximize detection power while minimizing main-task impact and susceptibility to ambiguity attacks requires further systematic study; and (4) embedding-location and robustness optimization — embedding the signature into low-level convolutional layers was chosen empirically because they tend to be less sparse, but the optimal selection of layers, signature sizes, and error-correction parameters (e.g., QR-code version and correction level) to maximize robustness against adaptive attackers remains an open practical question.
